title: 175-Year-Old West Bengal Temple Collapses Into Ganges as Erosion Breaches Barriers
excerpt: Severe riverbank erosion overwhelmed protective barriers and sandbag reinforcements around the historic structure, the second temple lost to the Ganges in less than a week.
body:
• A temple approximately 175 years old collapsed into the Ganges River in West Bengal on September 7, after severe erosion breached protective barriers in place since 1954
  • Local efforts to reinforce the area with sandbags failed against strong river currents, though no casualties were reported
  • The collapse follows the loss of Bihar's century-old Chaiti Durga Temple to Ganga erosion just five days earlier
  • Experts cite rising water levels, heavy silt deposition, and climate change as accelerating erosion along the Ganges

Temple Swept Away Despite Decades-Old Barriers

A temple dating back approximately 175 years collapsed into the Ganges River in India's West Bengal state on September 7, after severe erosion undermined the protective barriers surrounding the structure. The barriers, in place since 1954, could not withstand the force of the river's currents, according to Al Jazeera.

https://x.com/AJEnglish/status/2097086256853459250

Video of the collapse, broadcast by Al Jazeera and the South China Morning Post, showed the structure crumbling and sliding into the water. Despite local efforts to reinforce the area with sandbags, the strong currents overwhelmed the site. No casualties were reported.

The dramatic collapse shocked residents and raised fresh concerns over the vulnerability of heritage sites along one of India's most important rivers.

Second Temple Lost to the Ganges in a Week

The West Bengal collapse came just five days after Bihar's century-old Chaiti Durga Temple was swept away by Ganga erosion in Bhagalpur on September 2. In that incident, severe erosion at Raghopur swallowed large stretches of land along with the temple, a well-known religious site in the region.

Bihar Deputy Chief Minister Vijay Kumar Choudhary, who also holds the Water Resources Department portfolio, described the Bhagalpur situation as "challenging and difficult." He cut short a meeting in New Delhi and returned to Patna as the erosion intensified.

"The Ganga, in keeping with its natural course, has been causing erosion. The situation remains sensitive, and the department is making continuous efforts to bring it under control."

— Vijay Kumar Choudhary, Bihar Deputy Chief Minister

Water Resources Department Secretary Chandrashekhar Singh attributed the erosion to rising water levels, heavy silt deposition, and strong currents triggering erosion at several points along the river, according to PTI.

A Chronic Problem Along the Ganges

Riverbank erosion along the Ganges is a chronic and well-documented challenge. The Farakka Barrage, built at the river's narrowest point in West Bengal to divert water to Kolkata's port, has contributed to massive silt buildup upstream. The accumulated sediment has raised the riverbed significantly in some areas and forced the river to change its course, displacing communities and destroying structures.

Climate change is compounding the problem. Increased rainfall, rising water levels, and shifts in river flow patterns are accelerating erosion across the Gangetic plain. The loss of two temples within a single week underscores how vulnerable heritage sites and riverside communities remain despite ongoing protection efforts.

Emergency Response and Calls for Action

Engineers are evaluating the stability of the riverbank near the West Bengal collapse site to prevent further incidents, and emergency services remain on-site. In Bihar, the district administration has set up relief camps with food, drinking water, and healthcare for affected residents. Community kitchens have been established at multiple locations in Bhagalpur.

Local communities are calling for stricter monitoring of riverbanks and better preservation of cultural heritage sites. The government is expected to review its policies on infrastructure resilience in flood-prone areas.

What It Means for the Diaspora

Heritage sites along the Ganges hold deep cultural and spiritual significance for millions in the Indian diaspora, many of whom trace family roots to temple towns along the river. The twin collapses are a reminder that the physical landscape of cultural memory is itself under threat from environmental change.
